DETAILED ACTION
Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA  first to invent provisions.
Information Disclosure Statement
No IDS has been filed to date of the instant Office communication.
Priority
The effective priority date established for the present application is determined to be the actual filing date of the instant application, April 6, 2017 because the parent application does not have a proper support for a method involving a device having a plurality of sample inlet channels connected to a main channel carrying an immiscible carrier fluid.
Applicants are requested to point to the line and page numbers of the parent applications to which priority claim is sought for support.
Drawings
The drawings received on June 19, 2017 are acceptable.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(b)  CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph:
The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
Claim 8 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA  the applicant regards as the invention.
Claim 8 recites the phrase, “the droplets”.
It is unclear whether the droplets are referring to the droplets of the first fluid or those of the second fluid.  For the purpose of prosecution, it is assumed that the droplets of the both fluid are being referenced.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
(b) the invention was patented or described in a printed publication in this or a foreign country or in public use or on sale in this country, more than one year prior to the date of application for patent in the United States.
Claims 1-5, 9, 10, and 12-15 are rejected under pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 102(b) as being anticipated by Froehlich et al. (US 2014/0065631 A1, published March 2014).
Froehlich et al. disclose a system comprising the below structure (reproduced from Figure 5):
PNG    media_image1.png    390    697    media_image1.png    GreyscaleAs it can be seen, the device comprises a main channel (white arrow), which is disclosed as carrying an immiscible oil (“first reservoir (101) for uptake of a hydrophobic liquid … comprises at least one inlet (102) … with a first microfluidic channel (103)”, section [0011]), this inlet channel is equivalent to the main channel with white arrow indication of the flow direction.  The main channel carrying the hydrophobic liquid is then connected to a plurality of sample inlet channels (indicated black) injecting the samples therein into the main channel carrying the hydrophobic liquid, resulting in the generation of emulsion or microdroplet particles (“at least one element (110) comprising a second reservoir (111) for uptake of a hydrophilic solution ending in a vertical inlet (112) being opening into a second microfluidic channel (113) … connection between the first (103) and the second  microfluidic channel (113) is designed as a T-junction”, section [0011]).  This structure in the embodiment disclosed in Figure 5 (seen above) is the main channel with hydrophobic liquid which connects to a plurality of T-junctions form between each of the sample inlet channels with hydrophilic solution.
Therefore, Froehlich et al. disclose a method of providing a plurality of aqueous fluids in a plurality of inlet channels, providing an immiscible carrier fluid in a main channel, wherein each of the sample inlet channels is in fluid communication  with the main channel, and flowing a plurality of droplets comprising at least one aqueous fluid surrounded by the immiscible carrier fluid in the main channel.
Froehlich et al. explicitly disclose that the flow rate of the first channel is adjusted to control the droplet sizes (“flow rate in the first and second microfluidic channel is adjusted such that the diameter of each aqueous droplet generated within said first microfluidic channel ranges from 10 to 100 m”, section [0063]).
With regard to claims 2-4, Froehlich et al. also disclose that the pressure is applied to follow the immiscible fluid in the main channel (“means for providing a flow within said first microfluidic channel…”, section [0044]; “said first means is a pressure pump…”, section [0045]).
With regard to claim 5, the plurality of sample inlets result in generation of plurality of droplets comprising a first aqueous solution and a plurality of droplets comprising a second aqueous fluid (see Figure 5 above).
With regard to claim 9, the immiscible carrier fluid is oil (“said hydrophobic liquid comprise any oil”, section [0041]).
With regard to claim 10, the oil comprises a surfactant (“emulsion oils and optionally a surfactant”, section [0083]).
With regard to claims 12 and 13, the method involves nucleic acid amplification which is PCR (“present description is further directed to a system for digital PCR”, section [0048]).
With regard to claim 14, each droplet comprises one or more molecules (“said hydrophilic solution … mixture comprising a nucleic acid sample”, section [0040]).
With regard to claim 15, the one or more molecules are nucleotide (“hydrophilic solution comprises … dNTPs”, section [0040]).
Therefore, Froehlich et al. anticipate the invention as claimed.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
Claims 6-8, 16, and 17 are rejected under pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Froehlich et al. (US 2014/0065631 A1, published March 2014) in view of Cho et al. (US 2005/0202489 A1, published September 15, 2005).
The teachings of Froehlich et al. have already been discussed above.
While Froehlich et al. explicitly teach that the flow rate of the pump can be adjusted to control the droplet sizes, the artisans do not explicitly disclose that the droplets generated from the multiple inlet channels are of the same size or different size.
However, Cho et al. disclose a common knowledge in the art of emulsion PCR that the sizes of the droplets should be uniform when performing PCR (“the aqueous solution droplets have different sizes, which may cause a reproducibility problrm”, section [0015]; “since the reactant aqueous solution passes through the first inlet channel 141 with a constant sectional area at a constant flow rate, the aqueous solution droplets 132 created in the reaction channel 130 have a uniform size”, section [0081]).
It would have been prima facie obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made to combine the teachings of Froehlich et al. with the teachings of Cho et al., thereby arriving at the invention as claimed for the following reasons.
Initially, Cho et al. clearly evidence that when performing emulsion PCR, the emulsion particles should be of uniform sizes.  Therefore, given the fact that the method and device disclosed by Froehlich et al. are explicitly taught as being capable adjusting for the sizes of the droplets formed in the main channel carrying the immiscible oil, said one of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to keep the droplets generated from the single sample inlet to be kept uniform.
In addition, it is a common knowledge in the art that the concentration of the nucleic acids present in the droplets are also controlled by the size of the droplets.
“the concentration of nucleic acids within said sample is adjusted to provide at average one nucleic acid molecule per droplet … said sample is adjusted to one sequence copy in 1 to 100 pL …” (section [0064], Froehlich et al.)
“the flow rate in the first … microfluidic channel is adjusted such that the volume of each aqueous droplet generated within said first microfluidic channel ranges from 5 to 500 pL” (section [0062], Froehlich et al.)
Therefore, one of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to adjust the size of the droplets formed from each of the different sample inlets so as to control the amount of starting nucleic acid present in the droplets to optimize the amplification reaction for droplets generated from each of the different samples from their corresponding sample inlets, resulting in either the uniform sizes or different sizes (when comparing droplets generated from different sample inlets).
With regard to claim 8, the read-out instrument is a flow cytometer (“the read-out instrument is a flow cytometry instrument”, section [0050]).
Therefore, the invention as claimed is deemed prima facie obvious over the cited references.
Claims 11 and 18 are rejected under pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Froehlich et al. (US 2014/0065631 A1, published March 2014) in view of Kiss et al. (Analytical Chemistry, 2008, vol. 80, pages 8975-8981).
The teachings of Froehlich et al. have already been discussed above.
While Froehlich et al. disclose that immiscible oil is employed in generating emulsion droplets therein, the artisans do not explicitly disclose all prior art know variations of such immiscible fluids.
Kiss et al. disclose a well-known practice of employing fluorinate oil, such as fluorocarbon oil as the immiscible oil in generating emulsion droplets therein (“we describe a continuous-flow-based real-time PCR system that generates discrete, picoliter-scale PCR reations in a continuous stream of inert fluorinate oil”, page 8976, 1st column).
It would have been prima facie obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made to combine the teachings of Froehlich et al. with the teachings of Kiss et al. thereby arriving at the invention as claimed for the following reasons.
In KSR, the Supreme Court particularly emphasized “the need for caution in granting a patent based on the combination of elements found in the prior art,” Id. at 415, 82 USPQ2d at 1395, and discussed circumstances in which a patent might be determined to be obvious. Importantly, the Supreme Court reaffirmed principles based on its precedent that “[t]he combination of familiar elements according to known methods is likely to be obvious when it does no more than yield predictable results.” Id. at 415-16, 82 USPQ2d at 1395. The Supreme Court stated that there are “[t]hree cases decided after Graham [that] illustrate this doctrine.” Id.  at 416, 82 USPQ2d at 1395. (1) “In United States v. Adams, . . . [t]he Court recognized that when a patent claims a structure already known in the prior art that is altered by the mere substitution of one element for another known in the field, the combination must do more than yield a predictable result.”
Given the fact that fluorinate oil has been known to be used as an immiscible fluid in an emulsion amplification reaction, said one of ordinary skill in the art would have had a clear expectation of success that combining other well-known immiscible carrier fluid in the method disclosed by Froehlich et al. would have yielded the same predictable result of producing a successful amplification reaction.
Therefore, the invention as claimed is deemed prima facie obvious over the cited references.
Conclusion
No claims are allowed.
